q: Most common cause of a Bartholin Cyst?
a: Inflammation and obstruction of the Bartholin gland duct.

q: Classic clinical presentation of Lichen Sclerosus?
a: Thinning of the epidermis (parchment-like) and "leukoplakia" in postmenopausal women.

q: Risk of progression to Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Lichen Sclerosus?
a: Slightly increased risk.

q: Histologic hallmark of Lichen Simplex Chronicus?
a: Hyperplasia of the vulvar squamous epithelium and dermal inflammation.

q: Definitive cell type seen in Extramammary Paget Disease?
a: Large, malignant epithelial cells with PAS+, Keratin+, and S100- staining.

q: Key distinction between Vulvar Paget Disease and Melanoma?
a: Paget cells are PAS+ and Keratin+, while Melanoma is S100+.

q: Most common primary malignancy of the vagina?
a: Squamous cell carcinoma, usually associated with high-risk HPV.

q: Classic exposure history for Vaginal Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma?
a: In utero exposure to Diethylstilbestrol (DES).

q: Characteristic histologic finding in Sarcoma Botryoides (Rhabdomyosarcoma)?
a: Spindle-shaped cells with "cambium layer" and skeletal muscle differentiation (desmin+).

q: Defining feature of the Transformation Zone in the cervix?
a: Area where squamous epithelium meets columnar epithelium; site of most HPV infections. Uterus and Endometrium

q: Primary driver of Endometrial Hyperplasia?
a: Unopposed estrogen (obesity, PCOS, or exogenous source).

q: Most common symptom of Endometrial Carcinoma?
a: Postmenopausal bleeding.

q: Genetic mutation most associated with Endometrioid Carcinoma (Type I)?
a: PTEN tumor suppressor gene mutation.

q: Histologic characteristic of Serous Endometrial Carcinoma (Type II)?
a: Papillary growth pattern with Psammoma bodies and p53 mutations.

q: Definition of Adenomyosis?
a: Extension of endometrial glands and stroma into the uterine myometrium.

q: Definition of Endometriosis?
a: Ectopic endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine cavity.

q: Most common site for Endometriosis?
a: The ovaries (often forming "Chocolate Cysts").

q: Common clinical triad of Endometriosis?
a: Dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility.

q: Most common benign tumor in females?
a: Leiomyoma (Fibroid).

q: Characteristic gross appearance of a Leiomyoma?
a: Multiple, well-circumscribed, firm, gray-white whorled masses.

q: Key distinction between Leiomyoma and Leiomyosarcoma?
a:
Leiomyosarcomas are solitary, show necrosis, hemorrhage, and high mitotic activity.

Ovarian Pathology

q: Most common type of Ovarian Tumor?
a: Surface epithelial tumors.

q: Serum marker used to monitor response to treatment in surface epithelial ovarian cancer?
Most common malignant germ cell tumor in children?
a: Yolk Sac Tumor (Endodermal Sinus Tumor).

q: Characteristic histologic finding in Yolk Sac Tumors?
a: Schiller-Duval bodies (glomeruloid-like structures).

q: Tumor marker elevated in Yolk Sac Tumors?
a: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP).

q: Ovarian counterpart to the male seminoma?
a: Dysgerminoma.

q: Most common benign germ cell tumor in young women?
a: Cystic Teratoma (Dermoid Cyst).

q: Definition of Struma Ovarii?
a: A specialized teratoma composed primarily of thyroid tissue.

q: Most common clinical presentation of a Granulosa Cell Tumor?
a: Signs of estrogen excess (precocious puberty or postmenopausal bleeding).

q: Histologic hallmark of Granulosa Cell Tumors?
a: Call-Exner bodies (small follicles filled with eosinophilic material).

q: Definition of a Meigs Syndrome?
a: Triad of ovarian fibroma, ascites, and pleural effusion.

q: Definition of a Krukenberg Tumor?
a:
Metastatic signet-ring cell carcinoma to the ovaries, usually from a gastric primary.

Gestational and Placental Pathology

q: Genetic makeup of a Complete Hydatidiform Mole?
a: 46,XX or 46,XY (all paternal DNA; empty egg fertilized by two sperm or one sperm that duplicates).

q: Genetic makeup of a Partial Hydatidiform Mole?
a: Triploid (69,XXX or 69,XXY); normal egg fertilized by two sperm.

q: "Snowstorm" appearance on ultrasound indicates?
a: Hydatidiform Mole.

q: Risk of Choriocarcinoma is higher in which type of mole?
a: Complete Hydatidiform Mole.

q: Major hormone elevated in Gestational Trophoblastic Disease?
a: beta-hCG.

q: Characteristic of Eclampsia vs. Preeclampsia?
a: Preeclampsia (hypertension, edema, proteinuria) + Seizures.

q: Definition of Placenta Previa?
a: Attachment of the placenta to the lower uterine segment, covering the internal os.

q: Primary symptom of Placenta Abruptio?
a:
Painful vaginal bleeding in the third trimester.

Male Reproductive: Testis and Prostate

q: Most common risk factor for Testicular Germ Cell Tumors?
a: Cryptorchidism (undescended testes).

q: Most common testicular tumor in men aged 15-40?
a: Seminoma.

q: Histology of a Seminoma?
a: Large cells with clear cytoplasm and central nuclei ("fried egg" appearance) in lobules.

q: Tumor markers for Choriocarcinoma in males?
a: Significantly elevated hCG.

q: Most common testicular tumor in infants and children?
a: Yolk Sac Tumor.

q: Defining feature of Reidell’s cells in Leydig Cell Tumors?
a: Reinke crystals (rod-shaped cytoplasmic inclusions).

q: Primary location of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)?
a: Transitional zone (periurethral).

q: Primary location of Prostatic Adenocarcinoma?
a: Peripheral zone (posterior lobe).

q: Use of PSA (Prostate Specific Antigen) in screening?
a: Nonspecific; can be elevated in BPH, prostatitis, and cancer.

q: Most common site for Prostate Cancer metastasis?
a:
Bone (Osteoblastic lesions in the lumbar spine).

Breast Pathology

q: Most common cause of "Green-brown" nipple discharge?
a: Mammary Duct Ectasia.

q: Characteristics of Fibrocystic Changes (Non-proliferative)?
a: Cysts, fibrosis, and apocrine metaplasia (no increased risk of cancer).

q: Proliferative breast changes that increase cancer risk?
a: Sclerosing adenosis, ductal hyperplasia, and atypical hyperplasia.

q: Most common benign tumor of the female breast?
a: Fibroadenoma.

q: Characteristic clinical behavior of a Fibroadenoma?
a: Estrogen-sensitive (grows during pregnancy, shrinks during menopause).

q: Distinguishing feature of a Phyllodes Tumor from a Fibroadenoma?
a: "Leaf-like" projections and higher cellularity/malignancy potential.

q: Location of Intraductal Papilloma?
a: Within the large lactiferous ducts (typically presents with bloody nipple discharge).

q: Most common type of invasive breast cancer?
a: Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (No Special Type).

q: Histologic feature of Invasive Lobular Carcinoma?
a: "Single-file" pattern of cells due to loss of E-cadherin.

q: Clinical presentation of Inflammatory Breast Cancer?
a: Peau d’orange (orange peel skin) due to lymphatic obstruction.

q: Significance of Paget Disease of the Nipple?
a: Indicates underlying Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS). Infectious & Inflammatory

q: Causative agent of Syphilis?
a: Treponema pallidum.

q: Characteristic lesion of Primary Syphilis?
a: Chancre (painless ulcer).

q: Characteristic lesion of Secondary Syphilis?
a: Condyloma lata (flat, moist, wart-like lesions).

q: Causative agent of Lymphogranuloma Venereum?
a: Chlamydia trachomatis (L1-L3 serotypes).

q: Most common cause of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)?
a: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis.

q: Potential complication of PID involving the liver?
a: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis Syndrome (violin-string adhesions to the liver capsule).

q: Diagnostic finding in Bacterial Vaginosis?
a:
"Clue cells" (vaginal epithelial cells covered in bacteria).

Advanced Concepts & Syndromes

q: Common genetic mutation in Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS)?
a: Hyperinsulinemia leading to deranged LH:FSH ratio (>2:1).

q: Classic clinical pentad of PCOS?
a: Obesity, hirsutism, acne, infertility, and oligomenorrhea.

q: Association of Lichen Sclerosus with other diseases?
a: Autoimmune disorders (e.g., thyroiditis, vitiligo).

q: Role of High-risk HPV (16, 18) in oncogenesis?
a: E6 protein inhibits p53; E7 protein inhibits Rb.

q: Difference between a follicular cyst and a corpus luteum cyst?
a: Follicular arises from unruptured follicle; Corpus Luteum arises from a failed involution of the corpus luteum.

q: Histologic appearance of Medullary Carcinoma of the breast?
a: Sheets of large cells with prominent lymphocytic infiltrate (associated with BRCA1).

q: Most common cause of Scrotal Swelling in infants?
a: Hydrocele (patent processus vaginalis).

q: Mechanism of a Varicocele?
a: Dilated veins in the pampiniform plexus ("bag of worms").

q: Why are Varicoceles more common on the left side?
a: The left spermatic vein drains into the left renal vein at a 90-degree angle.

q: Definition of Hypospadias?
a: Urethral opening on the ventral (bottom) surface of the penis.

q: Definition of Epispadias?
a: Urethral opening on the dorsal (top) surface of the penis (associated with bladder exstrophy).

q: Definition of Bowen Disease of the penis?
a: In situ Squamous Cell Carcinoma presenting as a leukoplakic plaque on the shaft.

q: Major risk factor for Penile Squamous Cell Carcinoma?
a: HPV infection and lack of circumcision (poor hygiene/smegma).

q: Hallmark of Sertoli-Leydig Cell Tumors?
a: Re-masculinization or virilization in females.

q: Pathology of Brenner Tumor?
a: Ovarian tumor containing "Walnut-like" nuclei and urothelial (bladder-like) epithelium.

q: Definition of Endometrial Polyp?
a: Benign exophytic growth of endometrial glands and stroma; often associated with Tamoxifen.

q: Mechanism of fat necrosis in the breast?
a: Trauma-induced release of fatty acids leading to saponification and calcification.

q: Most common location for an ectopic pregnancy?
a: Ampulla of the Fallopian tube.

q: Definition of Asherman Syndrome?
a: Intrauterine adhesions (synechiae) following over-aggressive D&C, leading to infertility.

q: Cause of Vulvar Vestibulitis?
a: Inflammation of small glands in the vestibule causing severe entry dyspareunia.

q: Significance of a high mitotic count in a smooth muscle tumor of the uterus?
a: Suggests Leiomyosarcoma rather than Leiomyoma.

q: Common site of origin for Serous Tubal Intraepithelial Carcinoma (STIC)?
a: Fimbria of the Fallopian tube.

q: Histology of Comedocarcinoma (DCIS subtype)?
a: Central necrosis with calcifications within the duct.

q: Preferred staging system for Gynecologic cancers?
a: FIGO Staging.

q: Most significant prognostic factor in Breast Cancer?
a: Axillary lymph node status.

q: Effect of Triple Negative Breast Cancer on prognosis?
a: Poor prognosis (ER-, PR-, HER2-).

q: Hormone changes in Menopause?
a: Decreased estrogen, significantly increased FSH (loss of negative feedback).

q: Typical age for testicular torsion?
a: Neonates or adolescents (bell-clapper deformity).

q: Distinction between Seminoma and Non-seminomatous tumors regarding radiosensitivity?
a: Seminomas are highly radiosensitive.

q: Typical immunohistochemistry for Dysgerminoma?
a: OCT3/4, PLAP, and c-KIT (CD117).

q: Risk factors for Vulvar Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Non-HPV related)?
a: Long-standing Lichen Sclerosus in elderly women.

q: Definition of Chronic Prostatitis?
a: Recurrent UTIs or pelvic pain with/without bacterial growth in prostatic secretions.

q: Relationship between breast density and cancer risk?
a: Increased radiographic density correlates with higher risk.

q: Effect of breastfeeding on breast cancer risk?
a: Protective (decreases lifetime estrogen exposure).

q: Most common cause of Acute Mastitis?
a: Staphylococcus aureus (usually during breastfeeding).

q: Pathology of Periductal Mastitis?
a: Subareolar inflammation seen mostly in smokers (Vitamin A deficiency leads to squamous metaplasia).

q: Gross description of Mucinous (Colloid) Carcinoma of the breast?
a: "Blue-gray" gelatinous mass.

q: Precursor lesion to most Ovarian Surface Epithelial tumors?
a: Inclusion cysts or fimbrial epithelium.

q: Histologic feature of Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma of the ovary?
a: Large cells with clear cytoplasm and "hobnail" cells.

q: Definition of Endolymphatic Stromal Myosis?
a: Low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma that infiltrates vessels.

q: Definition of Decidualization?
a: Changes in endometrial stroma in response to progesterone to prepare for implantation.

q: Distinction between Squamous Cell Carcinoma and Adenocarcinoma of the cervix?
a: Both caused by HPV, but SCC arises from the exocervix and Adeno from the endocervical glands.

q: Common cause of spontaneous abortion in the first trimester?
a: Chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., aneuploidy).

q: Definition of Placenta Accreta?
a: Placental attachment directly to the myometrium due to a defective decidua.

q: Difference between Placenta Increta and Percreta?
a: Increta invades myometrium; Percreta invades through to the serosa/bladder.

q: Leading cause of Maternal Death in the developed world?
a: Thromboembolism or Preeclampsia complications.

q: Histologic marker for Choriocarcinoma?
a: Proliferation of cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts without villi.

q: Mechanism of Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn?
a: Maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and attack fetal RBCs (Rh incompatibility).

q: Definition of Hydrops Fetalis?
a: Severe fetal edema caused by anemia (immune or non-immune).

q: Most common benign neoplasm of the fallopian tube?
a: Adenomatoid tumor.

q: Clinical sign of Hydrocele?
a: Transillumination of the scrotum.

q: Presentation of Testicular Lymphoma?
a: Most common testicular mass in men >60; usually Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma.

q: Target of Trastuzumab (Herceptin) in breast cancer?
a: HER2/neu (ERBB2) receptor.

q: Precursor to Invasive Lobular Carcinoma?
a: Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS).

q: Management of LCIS?
a: Observation or Tamoxifen (considered a risk factor rather than a direct precursor).

q: Hallmark of Paget's Disease of the Vulva?
a: Intraepidermal spread of malignant cells; usually no underlying invasive cancer (unlike breast).

q: Most common cause of vulvar "strawberry spots" on the cervix?
a: Trichomonas vaginalis infection.

q: Characteristic feature of Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV) in the chronic phase?
a: Fibrosis and "esthiomene" (vulvar elephantiasis).

q: Primary histologic feature of Granuloma Inguinale (Donovanosis)?
a: Donovan bodies (intracellular safety-pin shaped bacteria) in macrophages.

q: Type of epithelium replaced in Vaginal Adenosis?
a: Squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar (glandular) epithelium.

q: Most common site for Vulvar Melanoma?
a: Labia minora and clitoris.

q: Defining histologic feature of Hidradenoma Papilliferum?
a: Complex papillary structures lined by a double layer of cells (myoepithelial and secretory).

q: Primary risk factor for Malignant Mixed Müllerian Tumor (MMMT)?
a:
Prior pelvic radiation therapy.

Uterus: Endometrium & Myometrium

q: Effect of Tamoxifen on the uterus vs. the breast?
a: Antagonist in the breast, but Pro-estrogenic (agonist) in the endometrium.

q: Characteristic finding in Chronic Endometritis biopsy?
a: Presence of Plasma Cells (lymphocytes alone are insufficient for diagnosis).

q: Common clinical consequence of an Inadequate Luteal Phase?
a: Infertility or repeated early pregnancy loss due to low progesterone.

q: Definition of Endometrial Metaplasia?
a: Replacement of normal endometrial glands with squamous or tubal cells.

q: Histologic feature of Endometrial Stromal Sarcoma?
a: Proliferation of cells resembling stromal cells during the proliferative phase.

q: Standard treatment for Endometrial Hyperplasia with Atypia?
a: Hysterectomy (due to high risk of progression to carcinoma).

q: Effect of oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) on Endometrial Cancer risk?
a:
Protective (progestin counteracts estrogen).

Ovarian Tumors (The "Small Print" Robbins Topics)

q: Classification of a Brenner Tumor?
a: Surface epithelial tumor with urothelial (bladder-like) differentiation.

q: Ovarian tumor associated with Pseudomyxoma Peritonei?
a: Mucinous Cystadenocarcinoma (often involving the appendix).

q: Primary difference between Serous and Mucinous ovarian tumors?
a: Serous are more often bilateral; Mucinous are more often unilateral and larger.

q: Defining feature of "Chocolate Cyst"?
a: Endometrioma (endometriosis of the ovary filled with old blood).

q: Tumor marker for Sertoli-Leydig Cell Tumors?
a: Testosterone (and potentially Inhibin).

q: Characteristic of Ovarian Fibroma Grossly?
a: Solid, firm, white, and whorled (resembles a uterine leiomyoma).

q: What is a Walthard Cell Rest?
a: Small nests of transitional-like cells on the fallopian tube/ovary surface (benign).

q: Most common primary cancer that metastasizes to the ovary?
a:
Gastric Carcinoma (Krukenberg) or Colon Carcinoma.

Gestational Pathology (Molecular & Rare)

q: Presence of fetal tissue in a Partial vs. Complete Mole?
a: Partial Mole contains fetal tissue; Complete Mole does not.

q: Risk of invasive mole or choriocarcinoma after a Complete Mole?
a: Approximately 15% to 20%.

q: Defining vascular change in Preeclampsia?
a: Fibrinoid necrosis and atherosis of the spiral arteries in the placenta.

q: Definition of Amniotic Fluid Embolism?
a: Entry of amniotic fluid into maternal circulation causing DIC and respiratory failure.

q: Histologic finding in Amniotic Fluid Embolism?
a: Squamous cells and lanugo hair in the maternal pulmonary microvasculature.

q: What is a Velamentous Cord Insertion?
a: Umbilical cord inserts into the fetal membranes rather than the placental mass.

q: Definition of Vasa Previa?
a:
Fetal vessels crossing the internal os of the cervix (high risk of fetal exsanguination).

Male Reproductive: Prostate & Penis

q: Gleason Score calculation basis?
a: Sum of the primary (most common) and secondary (second most common) architectural patterns.

q: Typical Gleason Score indicating high-grade, aggressive cancer?
a: 8 to 10 (Gleason Pattern 4 and 5).

q: Histologic marker absent in Prostatic Adenocarcinoma?
a: Basal cell layer (absent in malignant glands).

q: Effect of 5-alpha reductase inhibitors on BPH?
a: Blocks conversion of Testosterone to DHT, shrinking the prostate volume.

q: Term for "Hardening of the Penis" due to fibrous plaque in the tunica albuginea?
a: Peyronie Disease.

q: Define Erythroplasia of Queyrat?
a: Squamous cell carcinoma in situ (CIS) of the glans penis, presenting as a red plaque.

q: Clinical presentation of Bowenoid Papulosis?
a: Multiple reddish-brown papules on the penis; associated with HPV 16; rarely progresses to cancer. Male Reproductive: Testis & Scrotum

q: Serum marker often elevated in Seminomas?
a: Placental Alkaline Phosphatase (PLAP).

q: Is a Seminoma usually painful or painless?
a: Painless enlargement of the testis.

q: Tumor marker elevated in 100% of Choriocarcinomas?
a: hCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin).

q: Most common component of Mixed Germ Cell Tumors?
a: Embryonal Carcinoma.

q: Distinction between Embryonal Carcinoma and Seminoma?
a: Embryonal is more aggressive, often has hemorrhage/necrosis, and forms primitive glands.

q: Most common cause of Orchitis in a young adult?
a: Chlamydia or Gonorrhea.

q: Most common cause of Orchitis in an older man (>35)?
a: E. coli or Pseudomonas (UTI-related).

q: Unique complication of Mumps in post-pubertal males?
a:
Orchitis (can lead to infertility, but usually unilateral).

Breast Pathology: Molecular & Subtypes

q: Significance of "Radial Scar" on mammography?
a: Mimics carcinoma but is a benign lesion with a fibroelastotic center.

q: Defining feature of Sclerosing Adenosis?
a: Increased number of acini with stromal fibrosis and calcification.

q: Distinction between DCIS and LCIS regarding bilaterality?
a: LCIS is much more likely to be bilateral and multifocal.

q: Effect of HER2/neu amplification on breast cancer treatment?
a: Predicts response to Trastuzumab (anti-HER2 antibody).

q: Molecular marker used to predict benefit of chemotherapy in ER+ breast cancer?
a: Oncotype DX (multigene assay).

q: Triple Negative Breast Cancer is most common in which population?
a: African American women and BRCA1 mutation carriers.

q: Characteristics of Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS) cells?
a: Small, dyscohesive cells due to lack of E-cadherin.

q: Most common cause of Galactorrhea in non-pregnant women?
a:
Prolactinoma (Pituitary tumor).

Syndromes & Genetic Correlations

q: Genetic syndrome associated with bilateral ovarian fibromas?
a: Gorlin Syndrome (Nevoid Basal Cell Carcinoma Syndrome).

q: Association of Granulosa Cell Tumors with the endometrium?
a: Secreted estrogen causes Endometrial Hyperplasia or Carcinoma.

q: Mutation found in most Leydig Cell Tumors?
a: GNAS mutations.

q: Common karyotype of Klinefelter Syndrome?
a: 47,XXY.

q: Why does Klinefelter Syndrome cause high FSH?
a: Seminiferous tubule dysgenesis leads to decreased Inhibin B.

q: Primary defect in Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome?
a: Defective Androgen Receptor (X-linked).

q: Why do AIS patients have high LH?
a: Resistance to androgen feedback at the hypothalamus/pituitary.

q: Definition of Swyer Syndrome?
a:
46,XY karyotype with a SRY mutation resulting in a phenotypic female with streak gonads.

Diagnostics & Miscellaneous

q: Best stain to visualize basement membrane in the vagina?
a: Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS).

q: Use of Inhibin as a tumor marker?
a: Monitoring Granulosa Cell Tumors.

q: Diagnostic significance of a "Bag of Worms" on physical exam?
a: Varicocele.

q: Expected hCG level in a patient with an Ectopic Pregnancy?
a: Lower than expected for gestational age (fails to double every 48 hours).

q: Histologic feature of Condyloma Acuminatum?
a: Koilocytic atypia (wrinkled nuclei with perinuclear halos).

q: Term for fusion of labia due to low estrogen in children?
a: Labial Adhesions.

q: Primary cause of "Inadequate Luteal Phase" in older women?
a: Diminished ovarian reserve (failing corpus luteum).

q: Common cause of hematocolpos (blood in the vagina)?
a: Imperforate Hymen.

q: Defining feature of Turner Syndrome on the ovary?
a: Streak ovaries (accelerated oocyte loss).

q: Most common location for an accessory nipple (Polythelia)?
a: Along the milk line (axilla to groin).

q: Characteristic histologic feature of a Fibroepithelial Polyp (Skin Tag)?
a: Fibrovascular core covered by benign squamous epithelium.

q: Most common benign tumor of the vulva?
a: Condyloma Acuminatum (Genital Warts).

q: Definition of Vulvar Intraepithelial Neoplasia (VIN)?
a: Dysplastic squamous cells within the vulvar epidermis, graded I-III.

q: Primary treatment for high-grade VIN?
a: Surgical excision or laser ablation.

q: Relationship between Lichen Sclerosus and Squamous Cell Carcinoma?
a: Chronic inflammation leads to p53 mutations in the absence of HPV. Uterine Corpus & Tubes

q: Histologic appearance of Endometrial Stromal Nodule?
a: Well-circumscribed proliferation of endometrial stromal cells with no vascular invasion.

q: Distinction between Low-grade and High-grade Endometrial Stromal Sarcoma?
a: Low-grade has minimal atypia and infiltrates vessels; High-grade is pleomorphic and aggressive.

q: Primary cause of Salpingitis?
a: Ascending infection from the lower genital tract (Gonorrhea/Chlamydia).

q: Definition of Hydrosalpinx?
a: Distention of the fallopian tube with clear fluid, often following chronic salpingitis.

q: Most common benign tumor of the Fallopian Tube?
a:
Adenomatoid Tumor (mesothelial origin).

Ovarian: Specialized & Stromal

q: Characteristic clinical feature of a Hilus Cell Tumor?
a: Virilization due to testosterone production; contains Reinke crystals.

q: Defining feature of Gonadoblastoma?
a: Rare tumor found in dysgenetic gonads (e.g., Swyer Syndrome) containing germ cells and sex cord-stroma.

q: Most common source of Pseudomyxoma Peritonei?
a: Appendiceal mucinous neoplasm (rarely primary ovarian).

q: Pathogenesis of Ovarian Torsion?
a: Twisting of the ovary on its suspensory ligament, compromising blood flow.

q: "Bell-clapper deformity" is to the testis as ______ is to the ovary.
a:
An enlarged ovarian mass (dermoid or cyst).

Male Reproductive: Specialized Pathology

q: Definition of Phimosis?
a: Inability to retract the prepuce (foreskin) over the glans penis.

q: Definition of Paraphimosis?
a: Prepuce is trapped behind the glans, causing vascular compromise (medical emergency).

q: Typical presentation of Balanoposthitis?
a: Inflammation of the glans and prepuce, commonly in uncircumcised men with poor hygiene.

q: Most common type of Penile Cancer?
a: Squamous Cell Carcinoma.

q: Distinguishing feature of a Spermatocele?
a: Cystic accumulation of sperm in the head of the epididymis.

q: Histology of a Leydig Cell Tumor?
a: Eosinophilic cytoplasm with characteristic Reinke crystals.

q: Hormonal profile in a Sertoli Cell Tumor?
a:
Usually hormonally silent, but can rarely produce estrogens.

Breast: Rare & High-Yield

q: Characteristic of Diabetic Mastopathy?
a: Firm, painless breast mass in Type 1 Diabetics showing lymphocytic lobulitis and fibrosis.

q: Histology of Granulomatous Mastitis?
a: Non-caseating granulomas involving the lobules, often idiopathic or associated with Sarcoidosis.

q: Most common cause of a "Palpable Mass" in a woman under 30?
a: Fibroadenoma.

q: Definition of Atypical Ductal Hyperplasia (ADH)?
a: Proliferation of monomorphic cells partially filling a duct; increases breast cancer risk by 4-5x.

q: Common mutation in Familial Breast Cancer (other than BRCA)?
a: TP53 (Li-Fraumeni Syndrome) or PTEN (Cowden Syndrome).

q: Characteristic appearance of "Comedo" DCIS on gross pathology?
a:
Toothpaste-like necrotic material squeezed from the ducts.

Pregnancy & Placenta (Molecular)

q: Pathophysiology of HELLP Syndrome?
a: Severe preeclampsia leading to Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets.

q: Definition of Chorioamnionitis?
a: Bacterial infection of the fetal membranes, usually ascending from the vagina.

q: Gross appearance of the placenta in Chorioamnionitis?
a: Opaque, friable, and foul-smelling membranes.

q: Result of a "Circumvallate Placenta"?
a: A double layer of chorion and amnion creates a ring, increasing risk of premature rupture.

q: Primary cause of Abruptio Placentae?
a:
Maternal hypertension, cocaine use, or trauma.

Systemic/Syndromic Associations

q: Association between Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome and the reproductive system?
a: Increased risk of Sex Cord Tumors with Annular Tubules (SCTAT).

q: Ovarian tumor associated with Gorlin Syndrome?
a: Ovarian Fibroma.

q: Reproductive association with von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease?
a: Epididymal cystadenomas.

q: Genetic basis of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (most common type)?
a: 21-hydroxylase deficiency (leads to virilization in females).

q: Definition of Kallmann Syndrome?
a: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia (failure of GnRH neuron migration).

q: Relationship between Myasthenia Gravis and reproductive pathology?
a: Associated with Thymoma, which can be confused with germ cell tumors in the mediastinum.

q: Effect of Mumps on fertility?
a: Can cause permanent sterility if orchitis is bilateral and severe.

q: Most common site of extra-nodal Lymphoma in the male reproductive system?
a: The testis.

q: Most common oncogenic driver in Serous Cystadenocarcinoma (High Grade)?
a: TP53 mutation (present in >95% of cases).

q: Genetic mutation pathognomonic for Low-Grade Serous Ovarian Carcinoma?
a: KRAS or BRAF mutations.

q: Primary molecular defect in McCune-Albright Syndrome affecting the ovary?
a: GNAS gene mutation leading to constitutive activation of FSH receptors and precocious puberty.

q: FOXL2 mutation is a diagnostic marker for which tumor?
a: Adult-type Granulosa Cell Tumor.

q: DICER1 mutations are commonly associated with which pediatric ovarian tumor?
a: Sertoli-Leydig Cell Tumor.

q: The "Two-Hit Hypothesis" in BRCA1/2 related breast cancer refers to?
a:
An inherited germline mutation followed by a somatic loss of the remaining wild-type allele.

Specific Histological Variants

q: Classic histologic feature of "Hobnail Cells" is seen in?
a: Clear Cell Carcinoma of the ovary or endometrium.

q: Defining histological feature of an Adenomatoid Tumor?
a: Vacuolated mesothelial cells forming gland-like spaces (often in the epididymis or fallopian tube).

q: Presence of "Call-Exner-like" spaces in a male testicular tumor suggests?
a: Sertoli Cell Tumor.

q: Hallmark of Microcystic Adnexal Carcinoma of the vulva?
a: Deeply invasive nests of small cysts and cords with perineural invasion.

q: Definition of "Starry Sky" appearance in the reproductive system?
a:
Burkitt Lymphoma (can involve the ovaries or testes).

Advanced Male Reproductive Pathology

q: Term for the precursor lesion of most Testicular Germ Cell Tumors?
a: Germ Cell Neoplasia In Situ (GCNIS).

q: Which testicular germ cell tumor does NOT arise from GCNIS?
a: Pediatric Yolk Sac Tumor and Teratoma.

q: Primary immunohistochemical marker for Seminoma?
a: OCT3/4 and SALL4.

q: Histologic appearance of Spermatocytic Tumor (formerly Spermatocytic Seminoma)?
a: Three cell populations (small, medium, and giant) with "spireme" chromatin.

q: Typical behavior of a Spermatocytic Tumor vs. a Classic Seminoma?
a: Spermatocytic Tumors occur in older men and rarely metastasize.

q: Clinical significance of "High-Grade Prostatic Intraepithelial Neoplasia" (HGPIN)?
a:
Precursor to prostatic adenocarcinoma; requires close follow-up but not immediate surgery.

Clinical Correlation & "Pearls"

q: What is the "Schiller-Duval body" analogous to in embryology?
a: A primitive glomerulus.

q: Definition of "Pseudopityriasis Rosea" in the context of Syphilis?
a: The generalized maculopapular rash of secondary syphilis involving the palms and soles.

q: Cause of "Violin-string" adhesions in Fitz-Hugh-Curtis Syndrome?
a: Chronic inflammation and scarring of the liver capsule following PID.

q: Most common cause of a "Cold" (non-functional) nodule in the testis?
a: Any solid testicular mass should be considered malignant until proven otherwise (orchiectomy).

q: Significance of a "Blue Dot Sign" on the scrotum?
a: Torsion of the appendix testis (benign, non-surgical).

q: What is the "Whiff Test" used for?
a: Diagnosis of Bacterial Vaginosis (addition of KOH produces a fishy odor). Breast: High-Level Concepts

q: Definition of "Flat Epithelial Atypia" (FEA) in the breast?
a: Replacement of native terminal duct lobular unit cells by one or more layers of atypical cuboidal/columnar cells.

q: Most common cause of "Granulomatous Lobular Mastitis"?
a: Possible autoimmune reaction or reaction to Corynebacterium (seen in parous women).

q: Defining feature of "Inflammatory Breast Cancer" on biopsy?
a: Dermal lymphatic invasion by tumor emboli.

q: Histologic distinction of Medullary Carcinoma of the breast?
a: Pushing borders, syncytial growth pattern, and prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate.

q: Significance of the "Phyllodes" leaf-like architecture?
a:
Overgrowth of the stromal component relative to the epithelial component.

Placental & Developmental Nuances

q: Primary risk associated with a "Bipartite Placenta" (Placenta Bilobata)?
a: Increased risk of vasa previa and postpartum hemorrhage.

q: Definition of "Amnion Nodosum"?
a: Small, yellow-white nodules on the fetal surface of the amnion; associated with severe oligohydramnios.

q: Most common cause of "Single Umbilical Artery" (SUA)?
a: Usually idiopathic, but associated with an increased risk of fetal chromosomal and renal anomalies.

q: Pathogenesis of "Gestational Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia"?
a: Maternal antibodies (anti-HPA-1a) cross the placenta and destroy fetal platelets.

q: Characteristic finding in "Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia" (CIN) Grade III?
a: Full-thickness loss of maturation and high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.

q: IHC marker to differentiate Sex Cord-Stromal tumors from Epithelial tumors?
a: Inhibin (Positive in Sex Cord-Stromal).

q: Characteristic IHC profile for Embryonal Carcinoma?
a: CD30 positive, CK positive, and OCT3/4 positive.

q: IHC stain used to confirm a diagnosis of Mesothelioma in the tunica vaginalis?
a: Calretinin.

q: Use of p16 IHC in cervical pathology?
a: Strong, diffuse staining indicates high-risk HPV (E7) activity.

q: IHC marker for Clear Cell Carcinoma of the ovary?
a:
HNF-1-beta.

Clinical Syndromes & Drug Effects

q: Term for "Ovarian hyperstimulation" causing massive cystic enlargement?
a: Theca Lutein Cysts (associated with high hCG or fertility drugs).

q: Classic drug cause of Endometrial Polyps?
a: Tamoxifen.

q: Reproductive side effect of Spironolactone in males?
a: Gynecomastia (due to its anti-androgenic effects).

q: Condition of the breast associated with long-term Cimetidine use?
a: Gynecomastia.

q: Definition of "Stein-Leventhal Syndrome"?
a: The original name for Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS). Rare & Complex Variants

q: Definition of "Large Cell Calcifying Sertoli Cell Tumor"?
a: A rare Sertoli cell tumor associated with Carney Complex.

q: Defining feature of "Serous Surface Papillary Carcinoma"?
a: Primary peritoneal cancer that is histologically identical to ovarian serous carcinoma but the ovaries are minimally involved.

q: Histologic hallmark of "Microglandular Hyperplasia" of the cervix?
a: Proliferation of small glands, often associated with pregnancy or OCP use; mimics adenocarcinoma.

q: What is a "Decidual Cast"?
a: The entire thickened endometrial lining shed in one piece, often seen in ectopic pregnancy or sudden progesterone drop.

q: Definition of "Placental Site Trophoblastic Tumor" (PSTT)?
a: Rare tumor of intermediate trophoblasts; secretes Human Placental Lactogen (hPL) rather than hCG. Specific Developmental Anomalies

q: Definition of "Gartner Duct Cyst"?
a: Remnant of the Wolffian (Mesonephric) duct on the lateral wall of the vagina.

q: Definition of "Müllerian Agenesis" (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome)?
a: Congenital absence of the uterus and upper 2/3 of the vagina in 46,XX females.

q: Result of a "Bicornuate Uterus"?
a: Incomplete fusion of the Müllerian ducts, resulting in a heart-shaped uterus with two horns.

q: Origin of a "Paraovarian Cyst"?
a:
Remnants of the Wolffian duct located in the broad ligament (e.g., Hydatid of Morgagni).

Vascular & Inflammatory Extras

q: Most common cause of "Granulomatous Orchitis"?
a: Idiopathic (suspected autoimmune) or Tuberculosis.

q: Pathogenesis of "Fournier Gangrene"?
a: Necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum/scrotum; a surgical emergency.

q: "Yellow-brown" pigment in a "Luteoma of Pregnancy"?
a: Intracellular lipid.

q: Clinical behavior of a "Luteoma of Pregnancy"?
a: Benign, regresses spontaneously postpartum, but can cause maternal virilization.

q: Definition of "Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts" (SMULD)?
a:
Periductal mastitis; keratin plugs the duct leading to abscess and fistula formation in smokers.

Final High-Yield Odds & Ends

q: Primary risk factor for Primary Vaginal Melanoma?
a: Unlike skin melanoma, it is not UV-related; etiology is unknown.

q: Key difference between "Low-grade" and "High-grade" SIL (Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion)?
a: LSIL typically regresses (HPV 6, 11); HSIL has a high risk of progression (HPV 16, 18).

q: Primary symptom of "Torsion of the Appendix Testis"?
a: Sudden onset localized pain with a palpable "blue dot" on the upper scrotum.

q: Definition of "Prehn Sign"?
a: Relief of scrotal pain with elevation (Positive in epididymitis, Negative in torsion).

q: Most common cause of "Azoospermia" (no sperm) in cystic fibrosis?
a: Congenital Bilateral Absence of the Vas Deferens (CBAVD).

q: How to distinguish a Seminoma from a Dysgerminoma?
a: They are histologically identical; the name depends on the gender of the patient (Seminoma in males, Dysgerminoma in females).

q: Distinguishing feature of Embryonal Carcinoma vs. Yolk Sac Tumor markers?
a: Embryonal is usually AFP negative (or low), while Yolk Sac is always AFP positive.

q: Histologic hallmark of a Granular Cell Tumor of the vulva?
a: S100 positive cells with abundant eosinophilic granules and pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia (mimics SCC).

q: Primary difference between Follicular Cysts and Theca Lutein Cysts?
a: Follicular cysts are usually solitary; Theca Lutein cysts are multiple, bilateral, and driven by high hCG.

q: Key histologic distinction between Paget’s Disease of the Breast and Melanoma?
a: Paget cells contain mucin (PAS positive) and are S100 negative. Specific Molecular Pathology & IHC (Level 2)

q: Which breast cancer subtype is most associated with the "Basal-like" gene expression?
a: Triple-negative breast cancer (ER-, PR-, HER2-).

q: Primary molecular driver in Phyllodes Tumors?
a: MED12 mutations.

q: Molecular hallmark of Alveolar Rhabdomyosarcoma (Sarcoma Botryoides variant)?
a: t(2;13) or t(1;13) translocation involving PAX3 or PAX7.

q: IHC marker used to distinguish between a Complete and Partial Mole?
a: p57 (expressed in Partial Moles; absent in Complete Moles due to lack of maternal DNA).

q: Genetic mutation associated with Sertoli-Leydig tumors in Pleuropulmonary Blastoma?
a:
DICER1 mutation.

Placental & Umbilical Cord Micro-Pathology

q: Definition of Placental Infarction?
a: Localized necrosis of villi due to compromised maternal blood flow (common in Preeclampsia).

q: Histologic sign of a CMV infection in the placenta?
a: "Owl’s eye" intranuclear inclusions in enlarged villous cells.

q: Definition of Chorangioma?
a: A benign, hamartomatous capillary hemangioma of the placenta.

q: Significance of "Hoffbauer Cells" in the placenta?
a: They are fetal macrophages found in the villous stroma.

q: Consequence of "True Knots" in the umbilical cord?
a:
Can lead to fetal hypoxia and intrauterine fetal death (IUFD).

Clinical Signs & Eponyms

q: What is "Schwartzman Reaction" in the context of pregnancy?
a: A form of DIC and renal cortical necrosis triggered by endotoxins (often associated with septic abortion).

q: Definition of "Arias-Stella Reaction"?
a: Hypersecretory endometrial changes (enlarged nuclei) seen in pregnancy or ectopic pregnancy; mimics malignancy.

q: Classic presentation of "Peyronie Disease"?
a: Fibrous plaque in the tunica albuginea causing painful curvature of the penis during erection.

q: Definition of "Kraurosis Vulvae"?
a: Severe atrophy and shrinkage of the vulva, often the end-stage of Lichen Sclerosus.

q: Cause of "Pseudohermaphroditism" in males?
a:
Most commonly Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (46,XY with female phenotype).

Male Reproductive: Detailed Anatomy & Rare Tumors

q: Primary histologic feature of "Intratubular Germ Cell Neoplasia"?
a: Atypical germ cells limited to the seminiferous tubules (precursor to most GCTs).

q: Most common site for a "Sperm Granuloma"?
a: The eyeidymis (often follows a vasectomy).

q: Definition of "Tunica Vaginalis Hydrocele"?
a: Fluid collection between the parietal and visceral layers of the tunica vaginalis.

q: Mechanism of "Testicular Infarction" in Torsion?
a: Venous obstruction occurs first, followed by arterial compromise and hemorrhagic necrosis.

q: Histology of "Condyloma Acuminatum" vs. "Condyloma Latum"?
a: Acuminatum shows koilocytic atypia (HPV); Latum shows plasma cell-rich inflammation (Syphilis). Advanced Breast: Rare Findings

q: Definition of "Cystosarcoma Phyllodes"?
a: An older term for Phyllodes Tumor, emphasizing its "leaf-like" and potentially malignant nature.

q: Distinguishing feature of "Secretory Carcinoma" of the breast?
a: Rare, low-grade cancer that produces abundant intracellular and extracellular secretions; seen in children (Juvenile Carcinoma).

q: Common location for "Ectopic Breast Tissue"?
a: The axilla (most common site along the milk line).

q: Definition of "Mondor’s Disease"?
a: Superficial thrombophlebitis of the breast veins; presents as a painful, cord-like mass.

q: Significance of "Atypical Lobular Hyperplasia" (ALH)?
a: Similar to LCIS but cells fill <50% of the acini in a lobule; indicates increased cancer risk. Final Synthesis: USMLE "Must-Knows"

q: Most common cause of "Scrotal Pain" in a 20-year-old?
a: Epididymitis (usually Chlamydia or Gonorrhea).

q: Most common cause of "Scrotal Pain" in a 12-year-old?
a: Testicular Torsion.

q: Definition of "Hematocle"?
a: Blood in the tunica vaginalis, usually following trauma.

q: Result of "Chronic Endometritis" on fertility?
a: Increases risk of ectopic pregnancy and infertility due to tubal scarring.

q: Hallmark of "Postpartum Pituitary Necrosis" (Sheehan Syndrome)?
a: Failure to lactate and loss of pubic hair due to ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary.
